hints: Compare what is left after each acid loses a proton, the ethoxide ion $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$ and the phenoxide ion $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$, and ask which negative ion is more stable.
Think about what the lone pair on oxygen can do in phenoxide but cannot do in ethoxide, focusing on overlap with the benzene pi system versus the electron donating ethyl group.
walkthrough:
Decide which is stronger by thinking about the anions**
Acidity is all about how easily $\text{O-H}$ releases $\text{H}^+$. Picture both losing a proton: ethanol gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-$, phenol gives $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$. The more stable the negative ion, the further the equilibrium lies to the right, so the stronger the acid. Phenol wins here.

See why phenoxide is specially stabilised**
In phenol and phenoxide, the oxygen sits directly attached to the benzene ring. One lone pair on oxygen sits in a p orbital that can overlap with the delocalised pi system of the ring. That means the negative charge after deprotonation is not stuck on oxygen, it is spread over the ring. Spreading charge is stabilising, so the $\text{O-H}$ bond is weakened and more easily broken.

Contrast with ethanol**
In ethanol there is no ring to spread charge onto. The $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$ group actually pushes electrons toward the already negative $\text{O}^-$, which intensifies the charge and destabilises the ion. No delocalisation plus electron donation means ethoxide is much less stable, so ethanol is much less acidic.

Final answer: Phenol is more acidic than ethanol.
The lone pair / p orbital on O in the phenoxide ion is delocalised / overlaps with the pi system of the benzene ring, stabilising the anion and weakening the O-H bond. In ethanol the ethyl group is electron donating which destabilises the ethoxide anion.

hints: Recall that the $\text{-OH}$ group strongly activates the benzene ring, so phenol reacts under much milder conditions than benzene and gives 2,4,6 substitution.

For nitration, dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ at low temperature gives mainly mono substitution at the para position, while for bromination think about what form of bromine allows instant reaction without a Lewis acid catalyst.
Draw the products by keeping $\text{OH}$ at the top and placing $\text{NO}_2$ para to $\text{OH}$ for D, and three $\text{Br}$ atoms at the 2,4,6 positions for E.
walkthrough:
Use the activating power of phenol**
The $\text{-OH}$ group donates a lone pair into the ring, making phenol enormously more reactive than benzene toward electrophiles. You do not need concentrated acids or $\text{FeBr}_3$ catalyst. Mild conditions are enough, and substitution happens at the 2,4,6 positions where electron density is highest.

Assign D from dilute nitric acid**
With dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$ you get controlled mono nitration, mainly the para product. So draw phenol with $\text{OH}$ at the top and $\text{NO}_2$ opposite it at the bottom para position. That is 4-nitrophenol. Concentrated acid would give 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, so the dilute, cold conditions are key.

Assign E from bromine water**
Phenol decolourises bromine water instantly with no catalyst. Because activation is so strong, all three available 2,4,6 positions react. So the condition is aqueous $\text{Br}_2$, and the structure is $\text{OH}$ at position 1 with $\text{Br}$ at both ortho positions and the para position, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

Final answer: D is 4-nitrophenol: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ and $\text{NO}_2$ para to each other, formed with dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ at $5^{\circ}\text{C}$.
E is 2,4,6-tribromophenol: benzene ring with $\text{OH}$ at position 1 and $\text{Br}$ at positions 2,4,6, formed with aqueous $\text{Br}_2$ (bromine water, no catalyst, room temperature).

hints: Focus on what species attacks the benzene ring when $\text{Br}_2$ approaches phenol, and whether the ring keeps its aromaticity at the end.
walkthrough:
Name the ring mechanism**
The benzene pi cloud attacks an electrophile derived from $\text{Br}_2$, forms a temporary positive intermediate, then loses $\text{H}^+$ to restore aromaticity. Since an electrophile substitutes for hydrogen on the ring, the mechanism is electrophilic substitution.
Final answer: Electrophilic substitution.

hints: Remember how phenol gives a precipitate with bromine water and think whether the even more activated $\text{-NH}_2$ group in phenylamine will behave similarly.
walkthrough:
Link activation to observation**
Phenylamine has an $\text{-NH}_2$ group which activates the ring even more strongly than $\text{-OH}$. Like phenol, it instantly gives the 2,4,6-tribromo product which is insoluble in water. So you see the brown bromine water decolourised and a white precipitate appear.
Final answer: White precipitate / white solid of 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine.

hints: Recall why diazonium salts are kept in ice, thinking about what happens to $\text{HNO}_2$ and the $\text{Ar-N}_2^+$ ion if the mixture warms up.
walkthrough:
Keep the diazonium ion alive**
Nitrous acid is made in situ from $\text{NaNO}_2$ plus $\text{HCl}$, then reacts with phenylamine to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+$. This diazonium ion decomposes to give nitrogen gas if warm, so the whole reaction must be kept cold, typically $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ in an ice bath.
Final answer: Between $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ (ice cooling).

hints: Identify the two halves that join: the benzenediazonium part $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-N}_2^+$ and the phenol ring in alkaline solution.
Remember the coupling forms a $\text{N=N}$ bridge linking the two rings, with the link para to the $\text{OH}$ group on the phenol side.
walkthrough:
Build the azo bridge**
This is azo coupling. The electrophilic $\text{N}_2^+$ end of the diazonium ion attacks the activated phenol ring. The two nitrogens stay joined by a double bond, giving a $\text{-N=N-}$ bridge between the two benzene rings.

Place the rings correctly**
Draw $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-N=N-}$ attached to a second benzene ring bearing $\text{OH}$. In alkaline phenol the coupling occurs para to the $\text{OH}$, so the $\text{N=N}$ link and the $\text{OH}$ are opposite each other. That extended conjugated system is compound G, the coloured azo dye.
Final answer: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{-N=N-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-OH}$ with $\text{N=N}$ double bond between nitrogens and $\text{OH}$ para to the azo link.

hints: Count carbons in H, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{13}\text{N}$, and note H shows only three $^{13}\text{C}$ peaks because its two ethyl sides are symmetric, so J must also be a $\text{C}_5$ primary amine with symmetry giving only three environments.
walkthrough:
Use symmetry to find J**
Compound H is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{NH}_2)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. It has 5 carbons but only 3 peaks because the left and right sides mirror each other. You need another $\text{C}_5$ primary amine, so $\text{-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ or $\text{-CH(NH}_2\text{)-}$ or $\text{-C(NH}_2\text{)-}$, that also has only 3 distinct carbon types. The branched isomer $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ works perfectly: the three $\text{CH}_3$ groups are identical, plus one $\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3$ quaternary carbon, plus one $\text{CH}_2$, giving exactly three peaks.
Final answer: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{NH}_2$, 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-amine: central C bonded to three $\text{CH}_3$ groups and one $\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ group.

hints: Apply the n+1 rule: a doublet means the protons have exactly one neighbouring proton on the adjacent carbon, so look for $\text{CH}_3$ groups next to a $\text{CH}$ in K.
walkthrough:
Spot the doublet with n+1**
In K, $\text{(CH}_3)_2\text{N-CH(CH}_3)_2$? Actually $\text{CH}_3\text{-N(CH}_3)\text{-CH(CH}_3)\text{-CH}_3$, the $\text{N-CH}_3$ groups have no protons on the neighbour N, so they are singlets. The $\text{CH}$ has many neighbours so it is split into multiplets. The two $\text{CH}_3$ groups on the $\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$ side each see exactly one proton on the adjacent $\text{CH}$, so n = 1 gives n+1 = 2, a doublet. Circle those isopropyl methyl protons.
Final answer: Circle the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups attached to $\text{CH}$ (the isopropyl methyls, $\text{CH(CH}_3)_2$); either one or both circled.
